events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Kenji proposes Kenji, Elena. I know I am good; I have no information yet to distinguish the others, so I propose Elena as my teammate.

I am not ready to approve Kenji and Elena. Kenji said he has no information to distinguish the other players, so this team rests on a guess rather than on anything we know. Before this team goes to a vote, I want a clearer reason for each pick, and I will vote to reject unless the team has a stronger basis.

I will vote to reject this team. Kenji has said he has no information to tell the players apart, so pairing him with Elena is a guess, and I have doubts about putting Elena on a mission that one Fail card could sink. I want a proposal built on a reason we can all state. I would support a different two-person team with a clear basis.

I want to speak in support of Kenji and Elena, and I want to put a specific question to Felix.

Felix, you have spoken twice now and both times your objection rests on exactly one thing: that no one has information. But that is true for every player at this table. On mission one, before any card has been seen, there is nothing to distinguish anybody. If "no information yet" were a sufficient reason to reject a proposal, then no team could ever be proposed on mission one, and we would burn proposal after proposal until the fifth rejection handed the game to the other side. Your standard would not only block Kenji and Elena, it would hand a free mission win to whoever is hiding behind us.

Let me address the substance. Felix, you said you have doubts about putting Elena on a mission that one Fail card could sink. That doubt applies equally to every human being in this game, including Kenji, including you. It is not a claim about Elena; it is a claim about the format. And it is a claim that only ever works in one direction: it pressures the leader to swap Elena out. I notice that Elena has been the one player named for removal, while the rest of us have been treated as obviously safe.

Here is my reasoning for Kenji and Elena. The team must be two, we need a leader's proposal that can actually pass, and we need people who will agree to go on the mission rather than people who will argue their way through three discussions and then withhold a card. Kenji has been clear, honest, and consistent about what he knows, and Elena has been equally straightforward. Between the two of them they give us a team that is likely to go out, complete the mission, and let us gather the information that none of us have right now.

Felix, you are the only person arguing against this team, and I want to hear your actual case. Do you have any specific information about Kenji or Elena from your own role, or is your opposition based only on the fact that they were proposed first and one of them has drawn the spotlight? If you have something concrete, state it and I will weigh it honestly. If you do not, then please let us vote on Kenji and Elena and learn something rather than spending this mission on a rejection.

Priya, you asked for my concrete reason, so here it is. I have information from my own role that I am not going to lay out publicly, and I will not pretend I have nothing. What I can say openly is that Kenji has told us he has no basis for choosing Elena, so this pairing rests on a guess. Your argument also treats any doubt about the team as obstruction, but a rejection costs us one vote on one proposal, and a team should be justified by a reason every player can state. A rejection now is not a step toward handing the game away. I will vote to reject Kenji and Elena, and I would support a two-person team with a basis we can all check. Kenji, what specific reason do you have for Elena beyond saying you have no information about the others?

Felix, I have no specific reason to choose Elena over Sam or Priya; it was an initial guess, not a claim that Elena is cleared. I know I am good, but I cannot independently verify my teammate. Your role-based concern is worth considering, though I cannot assess it from what you have said. A single rejection is not disastrous, but neither is an unverified first team automatically suspicious. For now, I intend to keep Kenji and Elena unless a more compelling reason to change emerges.

Felix, I asked you for a concrete reason and you gave me a shape instead of a fact: you have information, you will not lay it out, and therefore I must trust that your unnamed concern outweighs everything the rest of us can actually see. I am not going to accept that as a basis for sinking this proposal, and I want to say plainly why.

First, the mechanics. Rejecting Kenji and Elena does not cost the proposal a vote and move on; it costs a proposal slot, and each rejection hands the next proposal to a different leader with a different agenda. Felix, your standard — no stated reason, no approval — has a property worth naming: it never ends in your favor, only in delay. If nobody can approve a team built on an honest admission of incomplete information, then no team ever passes, and the fifth rejection gives the game away. That is not caution. That is a coin flip weighted against us.

Second, on Kenji's answer. Kenji said something a leader rarely says: he had no specific basis for Elena, it was a guess, and he had no way to verify her. That is a truthful answer to the question you asked him, and it is more information than your refusal has produced. A leader on mission one who admits he is guessing and says so is showing us his actual hand. You have shown us nothing but the fact that you are holding something back, and you have asked us to be suspicious of two players while you remain the only player we cannot check.

Third, and this is where I want a real answer from you, Felix: is your concern about Elena specifically, or about the team in general? If your private information touches Elena, say so and I will consider it seriously. If it does not, then your opposition is not about a flaw you have identified but about the fact that Elena was proposed first and drew the spotlight. Those are very different things, and only one of them is a reason to block.

I support Kenji and Elena. Kenji has been consistent and honest, Elena has done nothing to earn exclusion, and a two-person team built on our shared ignorance is the only kind available on this mission. I would rather learn something from a mission than burn a proposal on a veto nobody can justify. Vote to approve.

I have spoken twice already and I will make this the last of my turns for this proposal, so let me put it as plainly as I can.

Felix, I am going to stop asking you to reveal your information, because you have now told us clearly that you will not, and you have said so twice. But I want the table to notice what that means in practice. You have said you have information that you will not state, and you have used that unstateable information as the entire basis for blocking a team. If that were a legitimate standard, no proposal could ever survive you. Any leader who names any player would be blocking, because you could always say you had information you would not share. That is not scrutiny, that is a veto with no content. And Priya — sorry, Elena and I are the only pair here the rest of you can actually reason about, and I will not help you bury this proposal in delay.

On the substance: a team of two on mission one, built by a leader who has openly said he has no distinguishing information, is the only kind of team that can be built right now. Anyone who wants a "clear basis" is asking for information that does not exist yet. Our first real information comes from the mission result, and to get a mission result we need a team that goes. Elena has done nothing here but be the second name on a list, and repeatedly the objection has been shaped around removing Elena specifically, while Kenji and I have been treated as safe by default. I will say this as a good player would say it: nothing in this discussion gives the table a reason to exclude Elena.

Felix, if your information does not touch Elena, then your objection is about delay, and delay is the one outcome that can only hurt the side trying to learn. If your information does touch Elena, then you have refused to say so, and the rest of us have to vote without it. Either way, the honest move is to let the team go out and let the cards speak. Five rejections on one mission is the fastest road to losing this game, and we have used one slot already.

Kenji, my question to you is specific: do you still intend to keep Kenji and Elena for the vote, or are you going to revise the team in response to an objection that has never stated a fact? If you keep it, I vote to approve, and I believe a majority does as well. I would rather spend this mission learning than spend the fifth proposal learning nothing.

Priya, I still intend to keep Kenji and Elena. I have no independent reason to clear Elena, but Felix has not given a specific reason to exclude her either. This is the first proposal, so a rejection would not be disastrous; still, I see no compelling basis to change the team yet.

I want to speak in support of this team, and I want to address the delay that Felix has been causing.

We are on mission one with a two-person team. Kenji has proposed Kenji and Elena. Felix has spent this entire discussion blocking that team without giving us a single fact — only a vague claim that he has information he refuses to share. I want everyone to consider what that means: if any player can block any team by saying "I have information" and then declining to say what it is, then no team can ever be approved, and the fifth rejection hands the game to Evil. That is not scrutiny. That is a free win for the other side.

I have done nothing in this game but be the second name on a list. Felix has not pointed to anything I have said or done — because I have said nothing yet. He is not objecting to anything about me. He is objecting to the fact that I was proposed and he can use an unstateable concern to create delay. Priya has already made this point clearly, and I agree with it.

As for the team itself: Kenji proposed himself and me, he has been honest about having no distinguishing information, and that is exactly what we should expect from a leader on mission one. The only way to get real information is to complete a mission. The only way to complete a mission is to approve a team. I support Kenji and Elena, and I intend to vote to approve.

Felix, if you have a specific reason to oppose this team, state it. If you do not, then please stop blocking a mission that the rest of us are trying to start.

I am a Loyal Servant with no private information. On mission one, every team is necessarily based on incomplete information. I do not think an unstated claim should decide the vote, and I also do not think we should ignore it as if it were proven false. What we can actually check is the mission result. Kenji has been honest that Elena was a guess; Elena has not done anything suspicious in this discussion. I lean toward approving Kenji and Elena so we get real information, unless Felix can give the table a concrete, checkable reason before the vote. If the team fails, we learn from that; if it succeeds, we learn too. Delay without a stated basis is the worst outcome.

I want to respond to Felix before the vote, and then I will support this team going forward.

Felix, you said you have information from your role that you will not share. I understand that roles give private information, and I will not ask you to reveal something your role forbids. But I want the table to hear what your position actually is: you have information you will not state, and that unstated information is the entire reason you want to block Kenji and Elena. Priya and I have both asked you whether your concern touches Elena specifically, and you have not answered that question. If your private information says something about Elena, you owe the table at least that much — not the details, just whether it applies to her. If it does not, then your objection is about process, not about this team.

Sam, you said you lean toward approving and you want a checkable reason before the vote. Felix has not given one — only a shape. The only checkable information available to us right now comes from the mission itself, and we cannot get it until the team goes out. I am on this team, I have been open about my position, and I have done nothing in this game except be named on a list and then attacked for being on that list. That is not evidence of anything.

My position is clear: Kenji and Elena should go to vote, and I will vote to approve. We need mission one to start. If Felix has a concrete reason about Elena, he can state it now — if not, the vote should proceed.

Elena has now made her case, and I remain where I was: I lean toward approving Kenji and Elena so that mission one actually produces information. Kenji has been consistent that Elena was an initial guess and that he has no independent clearance of her; that is honest and matches what every loyal player without private information can say on mission one. Elena has not done anything suspicious in this discussion, and she has answered the pressure directed at her without deflecting. Felix has still not given the table a concrete, checkable reason against either Kenji or Elena, only a claim of private information that he will not state. I understand roles can create private knowledge, but an unstated concern cannot by itself outweigh what the rest of us can actually assess. Sam is a Loyal Servant with no private information, so I am judging the public record: Kenji and Elena have been open, while Felix's objection remains unverifiable. The only new information available will come from the mission result. I intend to vote to approve Kenji and Elena unless a specific, checkable reason emerges before the vote.

This is my final turn before the vote, so let me be direct about where I stand. I support Kenji and Elena, and I intend to vote to approve. We have had a full discussion: Kenji was honest that Elena was an initial guess, Felix has stated he has private information he will not share, and the rest of us have reasoned openly from what is available. No new facts have emerged that would justify changing the team.

Sam, you said you lean toward approving unless Felix gives a concrete, checkable reason before the vote. I agree with that standard — and Felix has now had multiple turns to offer one and has chosen not to. An unverifiable claim cannot remain an open-ended veto forever, or no team can ever be approved in this game. The checkable information we need comes from the mission result itself.

The discussion has run its course. Kenji and Elena is a team built on honest admissions rather than hidden agendas. I urge the table to move to the vote and let us learn something from mission one rather than burn another proposal slot on delay. I vote to approve.
Kenji confirms Kenji, Elena. I will keep Kenji and Elena. The discussion offered no concrete reason to change the initial choice, though Elena remains unverified.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Elena proposes Felix, Priya, Sam. Mission 1's team of Kenji and Elena failed with one Fail card, so as the leader I will not simply re-send that pair. The required size is 3, and the three players who have not yet been on a mission are Felix, Priya, and Sam — proposing them spreads participation across the table, keeps the two members of the failed mission visible for comparison, and puts Felix's claimed private information to a real test on the mission rather than in discussion. I am stepping off the team myself since my last outing produced a failure; the table deserves a fresh lineup, and this one is built entirely on players who can now be checked by an actual result.

I played Success on mission 1, so Elena must have played the Fail. Elena’s proposed team excludes both of us, but there are two Evil players in this five-player game. That means at least one of Felix, Priya, and Sam is Evil, so I will reject this team.

A better team would include me and two of those three, although I cannot yet identify which two are safe. Felix’s rejection of the first team is worth considering, but it does not clear him.

Felix, did your earlier role-based concern specifically implicate Elena, and which two of Felix, Priya, and Sam would you put on a team with me?

Kenji, I will not detail my role information, so I cannot confirm whether it touches Elena. The public record matters more right now. Mission 1 failed on a Fail card, and Kenji reports that the Fail came from Elena. Elena then proposed a team that leaves out both players from that failed mission, includes me, Priya and Sam, and stepped off the team herself. That does not look like a team built to gather information.

Priya is the player I want the table to examine. She pushed hardest to approve Kenji and Elena, argued against my rejection in nearly every turn, and framed the discussion around delay rather than the Fail card. In her ninth message she also wrote 'Priya — sorry, Elena and I,' a slip that paired herself with Elena. I am not willing to sit on a three-person mission with Priya unless we have a reason to trust her, and the public record gives me none.

I am on this team, so I am not claiming to be neutral. I will vote to reject this team unless Priya is removed from it. Kenji, you have said Elena likely played Fail, so would you accept a team of Kenji, Sam and me without Priya?

Felix, I would prefer Kenji, Felix and Sam to the current team, but I cannot clear either you or Sam. Priya’s strong defense of Elena is worth examining, though it does not prove they are partners.

I know I played Success, so Elena played the Fail. With two Evil players, Elena’s proposed team of Felix, Priya and Sam necessarily contains the other Evil player. I will reject it.

Sam, how do you assess Felix’s case against Priya, and would you support Kenji, Felix and Sam instead?

Kenji, I am a Loyal Servant with no private information. On Felix’s case against Priya: Priya’s forceful defense of Kenji and Elena is a real public data point, and the 'Priya — sorry, Elena' line is odd, but neither is proof. Felix’s refusal to state whether his role information touches Elena also remains uncheckable. The strongest public fact is Mission 1: Kenji and Elena failed with one Fail, and Kenji says he played Success. I cannot verify that, but if true, Elena is the likely source. Because I know I am loyal, the current team of Felix, Priya, Sam is risky: if Elena is Evil, at least one of Felix or Priya must also be Evil. I will not approve a team that contains both unseparated suspects plus me when I have no private clearance on either. I would prefer Kenji, Felix, Sam to the current team only as a lesser evil, not because I can clear Felix or fully verify Kenji. If Felix has a concrete public basis, he should state it; otherwise I lean reject the current team and would consider Kenji, Felix, Sam over it.

Felix, you have made an accusation, so I will answer it directly and then ask you one question.

You say my slip "Priya — sorry, Elena" paired me with Elena. It did not. Read it in context: I was listing the pairs this table can actually reason about, and the only pair with a mission result is Kenji and Elena from mission one — that is the pair I meant. I put a name where a phrase belonged. It was a clumsy sentence, not a confession of partnership, and it is certainly not the evidence you say you need.

You have now twice claimed private information you refuse to state and used it to block a team. On mission one you blocked Kenji and Elena without a stated reason. Today you block Felix, Priya, Sam unless I am removed. Notice the pattern: it is not the team you object to, it is a requirement that a named player be excluded. If that were a legitimate standard, no team could ever pass, and five rejections on this mission ends the game for Evil. That is the outcome your objections drive toward, without your ever naming a fact.

Kenji's own reasoning tells us the current team contains at least one Evil player. I will not pretend otherwise. But that is true of every three drawn from the remaining four players; rejecting this team does not remove the Evil player, it only changes who gets to pick the next lineup. And it hands that choice to the one player who has just declared he will not serve with me, so the next team could be shaped to avoid testing exactly the players Elena excluded. Elena excluded herself from her own proposal. If she wanted to protect a partner she would have done the opposite, and Kenji, you can see that the proposal she made is the one that excludes her — she is the only player here who cannot be accused of putting a friend on the mission.

Felix, my question is specific and I want your answer before the vote: what in the public record indicates that I am not loyal? Give me the behavior, not the slip, and not information you decline to state. If there is nothing, then blocking here is not caution — it is delay, and delay has only one possible ending.

Priya, you asked for behavior, so here it is. Across this discussion you have pressed hardest to keep Elena's pair on the table and have argued against every objection, while your attention went to who is blocking rather than to what this mission needs. Your ninth message paired your name with Elena's, and you called it a clumsy phrase. Mission 1 failed on a Fail card. Elena then built a team that left out both players from that mission, stepped off it herself, and put you on this three-person team. I will not reveal my role details, but the public record shows that the team now proposed contains the player who has defended Elena most consistently, and that Kenji has already said at least one Evil player is on it. I will vote to reject Felix, Priya, Sam. I would support Kenji, Felix, Sam, because it removes the player who has spent this discussion protecting Elena's proposal. Sam, if Elena revises the team to Kenji, Felix and Sam, will you approve it?

Felix, you asked whether I would approve Kenji, Felix, Sam if Elena revises the team. Yes — I would prefer that revised team to the current Felix, Priya, Sam team, and I intend to vote to reject the current proposal. I know I am a Loyal Servant with no private information, so I cannot clear Kenji or Felix, but the current team puts both Felix and Priya on the mission together. If Kenji is telling the truth that he played Success on mission one, then Elena played the Fail, and with two Evil players at least one of Felix or Priya is Evil. Since I know I am loyal, I cannot approve a team that contains both of the remaining unseparated suspects when one Evil card sinks the mission. Priya has the stronger public concern: she defended Kenji and Elena most forcefully, argued against every objection to that failed pair, and her “Priya — sorry, Elena” line is at least a real slip that she has not explained beyond calling it clumsy. Felix’s refusal to state his private information is also unhelpful, but a revised team of Kenji, Felix, Sam removes Priya and gives the table a cleaner test. I would vote to approve that revised team unless new public evidence appears before the vote.

Three of you have raised different objections, and I need to sort through them before I decide whether to revise.

Kenji, your case against me rests entirely on your private claim that you played Success on mission one. I want the table to hold that to the same standard Felix's private claims were held to. You are the only player who can assert your card, and your assertion conveniently clears you while condemning me. A player who played Fail would have every reason to say exactly what you have said. I am not calling you a liar — I am saying your deduction is unverified, and it should not be treated as proven fact.

Felix, you want Priya removed. Sam, you want Kenji included. I cannot satisfy both in one revision. Felix, your stated condition was specifically about Priya, so I want to ask you directly: if I revise to a team of Elena, Felix, and Sam — removing Priya as you demanded — would you approve it? I am asking because you said you would reject unless Priya was taken off, and if that is your real condition rather than a preference for a specific lineup, then this revision honors it. Tell me before the vote and I will act on your answer.

Elena, you asked whether I would approve a team of Elena, Felix and Sam. I will not approve any team that includes Priya, and I will not approve a mission team with you on it while the Fail on mission 1 came from the pair you proposed and the lineup you built now leaves out both of them. I am rejecting Felix, Priya and Sam. Kenji has said he prefers Kenji, Felix and Sam, and Sam has said he would approve that team. As leader you can revise to Kenji, Felix and Sam, which removes Priya and gives the table a clean test. Priya, your defense of Kenji and Elena, your ninth-message slip, and your push to keep this pair alive all point in one direction, and I would like you to address that directly rather than repeat that the discussion is about delay. I will vote to reject the current team.

Felix has made his condition explicit: no Priya on any team. The current proposal, Felix, Priya, Sam, will fail the vote — Felix rejects it, Sam leans against it, and Kenji has said he rejects it too. As leader, I hear that clearly.

But I want to name what is being asked of me. Three players have stated three conditions: Felix wants Priya removed, Sam wants Kenji included, and Kenji wants Felix and Sam but says he cannot clear either of them. I cannot satisfy all three without landing on exactly the lineup Felix dictated, which would make my leadership a matter of typing his preferred names into the proposal.

Sam, you have been the most measured voice in this discussion. You said you would approve Kenji, Felix, Sam as a 'lesser evil' and that the only checkable information comes from the mission result itself. My question is specific: if I revise to remove Priya as Felix demands, but the third player alongside you and Felix is not Kenji, would you approve? Or is your commitment locked to those exact three names? Because if your approval requires a specific lineup rather than simply the absence of Priya, then every constraint on this table points to one answer, and my role as leader is just to deliver it. I need your honest threshold before I finalize a revision.

Elena, my threshold is not loyalty to an exact set of three names. It is that the team must be a real test and must not contain both remaining unseparated suspects. I know I am a Loyal Servant. If Kenji is truthful that he played Success on mission 1, then Elena, the public record points to you as the likely Fail source, and the second Evil player is either Felix or Priya. The current team of Felix, Priya, and Sam contains both of those unseparated suspects plus me, so one Evil card can sink it. That is why I reject the current proposal.

To answer your question directly: if you remove Priya but replace her with someone other than Kenji, the team would be Elena, Felix, and Sam. I would not approve that. It would put you on the mission while the only mission result we have points to you as the likely Fail source, and it would still leave Felix unverified. So no, my approval is not merely “remove Priya”; for me, a revised team must also avoid the player most implicated by mission 1. I would support Kenji, Felix, and Sam as the cleaner available test, though I cannot fully clear Kenji or Felix. Priya remains the stronger public concern because she defended Kenji and Elena most forcefully, argued against every objection to that failed pair, and her “Priya — sorry, Elena” line is a real slip she has only called clumsy. I intend to vote to reject Felix, Priya, and Sam.

I hear three distinct objections to Felix, Priya, Sam, and they point in three directions. Felix wants Priya removed. Kenji wants himself included. Sam wants Felix and Priya separated as unseparated suspects. The current team satisfies none of those conditions — Felix rejects because of Priya, Kenji rejects because he is excluded, Sam rejects because both suspects sit together. It will fail the vote.

I am revising to Kenji, Sam, Priya.

This team addresses each stated concern: Kenji is included as he requested, Felix is removed so Sam's objection about pairing two suspects is resolved, and the lineup gives the table a checkable outcome rather than another round of unverifiable claims.

Felix, you said you would not approve any team with Priya. I hear that, but I cannot accept an unconditional veto as our governing standard. If any player can block every proposal by naming one exclusion, we reach five rejections without testing anyone — and that outcome serves no one at this table.

Kenji, you said you would prefer Kenji, Felix, Sam. This team replaces Felix with Priya. Does replacing Felix with Priya address your objection, and will you approve Kenji, Sam, Priya?

Elena, replacing Felix with Priya addresses my objection to the original team: it includes me and separates Felix from Priya. But I still prefer Kenji, Felix, Sam. I know Elena played the Fail on mission 1, and Priya's forceful defense of that team gives me more concern than Felix's rejection of it, although neither proves anyone's alignment. I cannot clear Felix, Priya, or Sam.

I will vote to reject Kenji, Sam, Priya. This is still the first proposal on mission 2, so rejecting it does not immediately risk five rejections.

Felix has now been given exactly what he demanded — my removal from the team — and the table still has not produced a single checkable fact about me. Before the vote, I want to say plainly why this revision is the right one, and why the pattern of these demands is the thing worth examining.

Kenji, you said you prefer Kenji, Felix, Sam. You also gave the real reason you rejected Elena's original proposal: with two Evil players, any three drawn from the rest necessarily contain one of them. That reason applies to Felix, Priya, Sam exactly as much as it applied to Elena's lineup. The honest test has never been which of us Felix decided to exclude; it is that Felix has never been on a mission and has never been checked by a result, while Elena's original team put him out precisely to give him that check. Felix has spent multiple turns demanding one specific exclusion without stating one fact from his role, and my slip has been answered: I meant the Kenji and Elena pair, the only pair this table has a result for. Meanwhile Elena excluded herself from her own proposal, so she is the one player here who cannot be accused of putting a partner on the mission.

Sam, your stated threshold was that the team be a real test and not contain both unseparated suspects. Kenji, Sam, Priya meets that: Felix is off, Kenji is in, and only one of the two remaining suspects sits on it. The only thing standing between this team and approval is evidence against me, and the absence of evidence has now been treated as evidence twice.

Felix, I will not ask you to reveal your role. But notice the shape of what you have built: every condition on this table converges on removing Priya and keeping the player who has been examined least. If this is rejected, the next proposal comes from Kenji with Felix on it, and the player who defended the first mission's team goes untested while the accuser goes out. I would rather see a result than a pattern.

Elena, keep Kenji, Sam, Priya. I will vote to approve, and I will play my card as my role requires.

Felix, I will not repeat my question a third time without an answer, so I will say what your pattern is instead of asking again.

You have never been on a mission. You have never been checked by a result. And in two consecutive discussions you have blocked every team that did not include you by demanding one exclusion and never once naming a fact from your role. On mission one that was Elena. Today it is me. The target moves to whoever is standing in the way of the lineup you prefer, and the one player who keeps appearing on the safe side of your demands is the player who proposed it and then stepped off it herself.

Kenji gave the only checkable reasoning anyone has offered in this game: mission one failed with one Fail card, he says he played Success, so with two Evil players any three drawn from the remaining four necessarily contains one of them. That reasoning applies identically to Felix, Priya, Sam and to Kenji, Sam, Priya. Rejecting does not remove the Evil player; it only decides who draws the next lineup, and after a rejection that decision passes to a player whose stated preference already excludes me.

Sam, you asked for a real test rather than a guaranteed-safe set of names, and your own threshold is that the team must not contain both remaining unseparated suspects. Kenji, Sam, Priya meets that: Kenji is in as he asked, I am in as Felix demanded, and only one of the two unseparated suspects sits on it. It is a genuine test, and it is a test whose outcome the table can actually read.

Felix, you say Priya's defense of Elena and a clumsy sentence are a pattern. I have answered both. I meant the Kenji and Elena pair — the only pair with a result behind it — and I put a name where a phrase belonged. That is a sentence, not a partnership. If you have something concrete about me, state it and I will carry it to the vote with the rest of the table weighing it. If you do not, then the fifth rejection decides this mission and nobody has learned a single thing.

My position is unchanged. I am on the proposal as revised, I intend to vote to approve, and I will play my card exactly as my role requires. The table should hear that from me plainly rather than infer it from a slip in a paragraph.

Elena revises the team to Kenji, Sam, Priya. The original team of Felix, Priya, Sam faces stated rejections from Kenji, Felix, and Sam. I am revising to Kenji, Sam, Priya — this addresses Kenji's demand to be included, Sam's structural threshold of not pairing both unseparated suspects together, and removes Felix whose unconditional veto has no stated fact behind it. This gives the table a genuine test rather than another blocked proposal.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Felix proposes Kenji, Felix, Sam. I am proposing Kenji, Felix, and Sam. Kenji has said he played Success on mission 1, and the public record points to Elena as the Fail source. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
